plainMeaning: Highly refined wheat flour with the bran and germ milled out — low in fiber and micronutrients, with a higher glycemic impact than whole wheat.
healthNote: Common base of Indian bakery/snack products (biscuits, naan, samosa pastry); fine for occasional use but offers little nutritional value compared to whole-grain flour.

plainMeaning: A liquid sugar made by splitting sucrose into glucose and fructose — sweeter and more moisture-retentive than table sugar.
healthNote: Nutritionally equivalent to added sugar; used in bakery/confectionery to keep products soft and extend shelf life.

plainMeaning: A starch-derived carbohydrate powder, usually from corn, rice, or potato, used as a filler, thickener, or quick-energy carb.
healthNote: Digests almost as fast as pure glucose despite not tasting sweet — can spike blood sugar; common in processed snacks and sports drinks.

plainMeaning: A sweetener made by processing corn starch into a syrup of glucose and fructose.
healthNote: Functions in the body like other added sugars; frequently used in sodas, sauces, and packaged desserts for cost and shelf-stability.

plainMeaning: Vegetable oil chemically hardened by adding hydrogen, turning liquid oil into a solid/semi-solid fat.
healthNote: Partial hydrogenation can produce trans fats, linked to cardiovascular risk; India (FSSAI) caps industrial trans fat at 2% of total fat in food (2022 rules), but check the label's trans-fat line.

plainMeaning: An oil pressed from the fruit of the oil palm, high in saturated fat and semi-solid at room temperature.
healthNote: Not a trans fat source, but high in saturated fat; widely used in packaged snacks for its low cost and long shelf life.

plainMeaning: A synthetic preservative that stops mould, yeast, and some bacteria from growing in acidic foods and drinks.
healthNote: Approved within FSSAI limits; can form small amounts of benzene when combined with vitamin C under heat/light, though regulated levels are considered safe.

plainMeaning: A synthetic preservative that inhibits mould and yeast growth, commonly used in place of sodium benzoate.
healthNote: Generally regarded as one of the milder preservatives; approved within FSSAI limits.

plainMeaning: The sodium salt of glutamic acid, an amino acid — added purely to intensify savoury (umami) taste.
healthNote: Considered safe by FSSAI/international food-safety bodies at normal intake levels, despite popular concern; adds no nutritional value.

plainMeaning: A sulphite preservative that prevents browning and inhibits microbial growth, often in dried fruit or packaged juices.
healthNote: Can trigger reactions in people with sulphite sensitivity or asthma; must be declared as an allergen-relevant additive.

plainMeaning: A synthetic antioxidant added to oils and fried snacks to stop fats from turning rancid.
healthNote: Approved within strict FSSAI limits; used in small quantities specifically to extend shelf life of fried/oily packaged foods.

plainMeaning: A curing salt used in processed/packaged meats to fix colour and block bacterial growth (notably botulism).
healthNote: Can react with proteins during high-heat cooking to form nitrosamines, which health bodies advise limiting; mainly relevant to cured/processed meat products.

plainMeaning: A synthetic, very low-calorie artificial sweetener roughly 200x sweeter than sugar.
healthNote: Approved within FSSAI limits; not suitable for people with the rare genetic condition phenylketonuria (PKU), as it contains phenylalanine.

plainMeaning: A synthetic, zero-calorie artificial sweetener made from sugar, roughly 600x sweeter than sugar.
healthNote: Passes through the body largely unabsorbed; approved within FSSAI limits for 'diet'/low-sugar products.

plainMeaning: A synthetic, zero-calorie artificial sweetener often blended with other sweeteners to round out taste.
healthNote: Approved within FSSAI limits; commonly paired with sucralose or aspartame in 'diet' beverages.

aliases: mono and diglycerides of fatty acids
plainMeaning: Emulsifiers made from fats that help oil and water mix evenly, keeping baked goods soft and batters smooth.
healthNote: Very widely used and generally considered safe; can occasionally be derived from animal fat, relevant to strict vegetarians unless labelled plant-sourced.

plainMeaning: A natural emulsifier (often from soy or sunflower) that keeps fat and water blended, e.g. in chocolate or bakery products.
healthNote: Generally well tolerated; relevant as a soy-allergen flag if soy-derived and not otherwise disclosed.

plainMeaning: A thickener/stabilizer extracted from red seaweed, used to give dairy and dairy-alternative products body.
healthNote: Approved food-grade additive; distinct from 'poligeenan' (a degraded form studied for gut irritation) which is not permitted in food.

plainMeaning: A fermentation-derived thickener that gives sauces, dressings, and gluten-free baked goods a stable texture.
healthNote: Widely regarded as safe; adds negligible calories and no nutritional concern at typical use levels.

plainMeaning: A synthetic yellow food dye used purely for colour, with no flavour or nutritional function.
healthNote: Some studies link azo dyes like tartrazine to hyperactivity in sensitive children; FSSAI permits it within set limits and it must be declared on-label.

plainMeaning: A synthetic orange-yellow food dye used purely for colour.
healthNote: Another azo dye flagged in some hyperactivity studies; permitted by FSSAI within set limits.

plainMeaning: A synthetic red/pink food dye used purely for colour, common in glace cherries and some confectionery.
healthNote: Permitted by FSSAI within set limits; some regulators have restricted its use pending safety review.

plainMeaning: Corn syrup with the water removed to form a powder — still functions as an added sugar.
healthNote: Nutritionally behaves like added sugar despite the less obviously 'sugary' name; common in powdered mixes and creamers.

plainMeaning: Pure glucose sugar, chemically identical to the glucose in your bloodstream — the fastest-absorbed common sugar.
healthNote: Causes a rapid blood-sugar rise; used in packaged foods for sweetness, browning, or as a cheap bulking agent.

plainMeaning: Plant protein broken down chemically into amino acids, used as a savoury flavour booster similar in effect to MSG.
healthNote: Naturally high in free glutamate, so it acts like an MSG substitute; the source crop (often soy or wheat) matters for allergen labelling.

plainMeaning: A leavening agent that releases gas when heated, used in flat, crisp baked goods like some biscuits and crackers.
healthNote: Fully decomposes and bakes off during cooking, leaving no residue of concern; long-standing traditional raising agent.

plainMeaning: A mould-inhibiting preservative commonly used in packaged bread.
healthNote: Approved within FSSAI limits; occasionally associated with headaches or irritability in sensitive individuals, though evidence is limited.

plainMeaning: A synthetic antioxidant added to fats and oils to prevent them from going rancid and to extend shelf life.
healthNote: Permitted within FSSAI limits; some international bodies classify it as a possible carcinogen at high doses, prompting several brands to phase it out.
